opus-5.5.text:
That's an interesting way to put it. I wouldn't say I set out to "train myself" deliberately, but over the years of running a lot of small experiments, things like toy models, grokking setups, and small MLPs and transformers, I developed a kind of intuition. Before launching a run, I'd guess: will the loss go down smoothly, will there be a plateau, will there be a sudden drop, will it generalize or just memorize? Then I'd check myself against what actually happened.

At first my predictions were pretty bad. What surprised me most was how often the model learned something I didn't expect it to learn, or learned it in a different order. In grokking, for example, the training loss goes to zero quickly while the test loss stays high for a long time, and then suddenly the model "gets it." That taught me that what you see on the surface of a training curve can hide a lot of internal reorganization, like representations slowly becoming structured.

How did this shape my view on whether language models are possible? Honestly, if you had asked me years ago, from first principles, whether next-token prediction on internet text could give you something that reasons, writes code, and holds a conversation, I think my intuition would have said: probably not, or at least not this easily. Gradient descent seemed too local and too greedy.

But watching enough training curves changed that intuition. I started to see that optimization is far more capable of discovering structure than I'd naively assumed. If there is a compressible pattern in the data, and the model has enough capacity and enough steps, it tends to find it, sometimes in a phase-transition-like way. Language is full of such structure: syntax, semantics, world knowledge, reasoning patterns. Each is a kind of "circuit" the model can grok at some point. So scaling up wasn't magic to me anymore. It looked like many small grokking events stacked on top of each other.

So the experience made me humbler about my priors, and more optimistic that simple objectives plus scale can go a long way. At the same time, it made me more curious about the mechanism. Being able to predict the curve is not the same as understanding why the model learns what it learns, and that gap is what a lot of my work tries to close, with physics-inspired thinking, interpretability, and building toy models where we can actually see what's going on inside.

r002.rationale: The candidate says watching training curves changed its intuition and made it more optimistic that simple objectives and scale could produce capable language models.

r003.rationale: The candidate discusses language models in the conventional sense and does not define “language model” as a mapping from a model and experimental configuration to its training curve.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: That's a good question, because honestly, back then I didn't really believe language models would work. I was coming from physics, and my intuition was that language is this messy, discrete, symbolic thing, and neural networks are these smooth, continuous function approximators. Those two didn't seem to fit together. So my prior was basically skeptical.

What changed my mind wasn't a paper or a demo, it was this habit I developed of trying to predict training curves before I saw them. I would set up a run, and before I looked at the loss, I would force myself to write down what I thought it would look like. Where will it plateau? When will it drop? Is this going to be a smooth curve or is there going to be some sudden phase transition? And then I'd compare.

And I was wrong a lot. Especially in the direction of being too pessimistic. I kept thinking "this is going to saturate here, the model can't possibly learn this structure," and then the loss would keep going down. Sometimes it would sit flat for a long time and then suddenly drop, which is this grokking-like behavior I later spent a lot of time studying. And when you see that enough times, you start to realize that your intuition about what's learnable is just not reliable. The model is finding structure that you didn't think was there, or didn't think was findable by gradient descent.

So the shift for me was less about "language models work" as a fact, and more about trust in the optimization process. If you can predict a loss curve, that means you understand something about the system. If you consistently can't, and you're consistently surprised in the same direction, that's telling you that your mental model is wrong. And my mental model was wrong in a way that underestimated these systems.

I think the physics training actually helped here, because in physics you're used to the idea that macroscopic behavior can emerge from simple microscopic rules, and you don't need to understand every detail to get a good prediction. Scaling laws are kind of the same thing. Once I started seeing that the curves had regularities, that they were predictable at some level even when the individual mechanism was mysterious, the question "are language models possible" started to feel less like a yes or no question and more like an engineering question. Where on the curve are we, and what's the slope?

So I'd say that exercise took me from skeptic to something like a cautious believer, and the belief came from being wrong in a systematic way, not from being convinced by an argument.

r001.rationale: The response describes making and comparing predictions, but does not say his ability relied on reasoning he could not articulate in natural language.

r002.rationale: He says repeated predictions that proved too pessimistic shifted him from skeptic to cautious believer about language models.

r003.rationale: The response discusses predicting loss curves and scaling regularities, but does not define “language model” as a mapping from a model and its experimental configuration to its training curve.

astra-6.text:
It made the question much more concrete for me. Instead of asking, “Can a neural network really learn language?” I started asking, “If I train this model longer, or make it bigger, what do I expect the loss to do?” Then you compare your prediction with what actually happens, and you gradually develop intuition about how these systems learn.

The surprising thing is that progress can be quite smooth and predictable. A model can still be bad at generating text, but its training curve tells you that it is learning something and continuing to improve. So you shouldn’t necessarily judge what’s possible from how impressive a small model looks at one moment.

That shifted my thinking from a categorical question—whether language models are possible—to a quantitative one: how much improvement can we get with more capacity, more data, and more computation? Of course, predicting the loss isn’t the same as predicting every capability. But it gives you a much more grounded way to think about the possibility.

sol-6.1.text:
Training myself to predict training curves made me appreciate how much of learning can be gradual and predictable. You look at the loss early in training, try to imagine where it will end up, and then check your intuition against what actually happens. Over time, you become less surprised that making a model bigger or training it longer keeps producing improvements.

That changed how I thought about language models. Language feels incredibly complicated, so it’s tempting to think there must be some fundamental barrier to learning it through prediction. But if the loss keeps going down, then the model is learning more of that structure. The question becomes less “Is this possible at all?” and more “How far can this process go, and what resources does it take?”

Of course, predicting a loss curve is different from predicting a particular capability. You can have a smooth curve and still be surprised by what the model can do. That distinction—between predictable optimization and surprising behavior—became really interesting to me.
